A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–E. Corresponding content can be matched despite added experiments and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original embedding-condensation measurements, mid-training and pre-training benchmark results, and hyperparameter ablations in Figures 2–4 and 6 and Tables 2–4.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds controlled model-size experiments, additional training comparisons, and layer-placement ablations, including Figure 3 and Tables 2–3.

M1.justification: Appendix A changes Algorithm 1 from ordinary epsilon-based clamping to a separate clamp threshold and a detached correction that preserves boundary gradients beyond the clamp instead of zeroing them. This changes the documented optimization procedure locally; the dispersion objective, architecture, and three alternative losses remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds codelion/fineweb-edu-1B as a training corpus for the controlled model-size experiment (Table S1). The ten downstream benchmarks and existing WikiText/C4 training coverage remain. PubMedQA, IMDb, and SQuAD were already described as used in v1; their new plots do not establish newly added coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated noisy-embedding and active-forgetting comparators, inspired by Jain et al. (2024) and Chen et al. (2023), to the existing mid-training comparisons. This substantially broadens comparison beyond default training and the authors' three alternative loss formulations, which are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds controlled MLP-width pre-training, Qwen3-1.7B mid-training, selective layer regularization, average ranks, and last-layer cosine metrics. Table S1 also changes GPT2-m's stated learning rate from 5e-6 to 5e-5 and revises microbatch sizes and gradient accumulation while retaining effective batch sizes. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish whether existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a model-size study holding depth, embedding dimension, and training conditions fixed (Figure 3), plus an early-versus-late-layer dispersion ablation (Table 3). Appendix C adds plotted evidence for previously described cross-corpus robustness and an alternative-metric analysis (Figures S2–S3). The original hyperparameter sweep remains as Table 4.

E5.justification: V1 reports benchmark point estimates without training-seed counts, standard deviations, or significance tests. V2 specifies three random seeds for mid-training and reports means, standard deviations, and Student's t-tests in Tables 2–3. This is substantial new statistical reporting, not evidence of an increase from a known v1 run count; pre-training results remain point estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial result entries for new comparators, controlled models, and supplementary analyses. Newly mid-trained Qwen3-1.7B scores 55.68 with dispersion versus 54.57 with default training (Table 2); later-layer versus earlier-layer regularization scores 35.37 versus 34.96 (Table 3). Previously reported benchmark values are retained, including pre-training averages of 34.84 and 36.01.

T1.justification: Definitions 1.1–1.2, the loss formulations, and the mathematical content of Appendices D–E are retained, including Propositions E.1–E.2 and their proofs. The additional cosine-similarity evaluation introduces no substantive new formal definition, theorem, or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims about condensation, model size, distillation, and dispersion training. The introduction corrects the claimed pre-training improvement from +1.07 and 3.1% to +1.17 and 3.3%; the +1.17 table result already appeared in v1.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the controlled study and layer ablation as stronger support for the proposed mechanism. It adds explanations for weaker alternative losses and suggests greater benefits on knowledge-heavy tasks than on WinoGrande. It also replaces deferred quadratic-cost optimization with discussion of manageable cost through token subsampling. These extend the retained interpretation without broadly redefining applicability.

D1.justification: V2 adds code-repository and project-page links, per-method A100 training hours and overhead ratios in Table 2, and configurations for the controlled experiment and Qwen3-1.7B in Table S1. Appendix A documents the revised gradient handling, and the main text discusses token subsampling. Together these substantially expand implementation, resource, and access information.

R1.justification: V2 adds relevant work by Li and Tokarchuk and explicitly distinguishes its layer-wise analysis and broad benchmark evaluation from concurrent dispersion work focused on perplexity. It also cites the new comparison methods and corrects TruthfulQA's attribution to Lin et al. (2022). These are focused additions to the existing positioning.

P1.justification: V2 merges the standalone preliminaries into Methods, nests the hyperparameter discussion within mid-training, subdivides Appendix C, and adds acknowledgements. It clarifies contextualized embeddings and corrects terminology and wording, including TrustfulQA to TruthfulQA. Most original prose and the overall narrative sequence remain.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 3, Figures S2–S3, and the layer-ablation Table 3. Table 2 is substantially redesigned with more rows, uncertainty, training-time, rank, and significance columns; Table S1 gains experimental columns. Figure 1 is redrawn, while several existing figures and tables are relocated or renumbered rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument. The controlled model-size experiment and layer-placement ablation address weaknesses in attributing effects to condensation, while independent comparators and three-seed uncertainty reporting make the modest performance gains more assessable. Timing and access information also improve reproducibility. Some GPT2 comparisons remain nonsignificant and pre-training lacks uncertainty estimates, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support.
